articles.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
articles.summary: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64

top_comments: From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.And the "Limitations" section:> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

Super impressive work by Calif as usual.The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here: https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2...They look for these five conditions: * HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9 and GCJ are OK. Azul Prime (Zing), which replaces C2 with its own JIT, and any VM name not recognized as HotSpot are [?], never [!]. * x86-64 JVM on an x86-64 host. * Version 17.0.6 or later, not at or above a version listed in FIXED_IN, and no newer than the newest releases checked (see below). Newer versions are [?]: they may carry the fix. * The JVM reports avx512_vbmi and avx512bw, and UseAVX >= 3. * Base64 intrinsics are on and C2/JVMCI can compile. These turn it off: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, -Xint, -XX:TieredStopAtLevel below 4.

What’s that old Chinese proverb? “May you live in interesting times”? It feels like we’re living in interesting times. How long will it take for a bad actor to seriously compromise critical infrastructure? My bet is within six months.The upside is that it’ll force legacy institutions and organizations with sub-par security to get good at security and modernize their legacy stacks. That, or get pwned in short order.

articles.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.summary: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine

top_comments: (context: I'm the CTO at Quad9) It's really great seeing the support from other organizations in the same space as Quad9 on this topic. Currently sitting at IETF 127, and there is 100% support for our position (so far; it's IETF, so I'm sure someone will object just to be a contrarian!) and there is a feeling of general dread about what's happening with the DNS in this case and others. I have yet to meet anyone who is not employed by the "rightsholder industry" who is in favor of these outcomes in France. Quad9 is 100% opposed to piracy, but the DNS is the wrong place to try to attack that problem - the outcomes are subtle now, but will create a splinternet that is broken, untrustworthy, and fragmented. The EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region - this is a really bad example and it should not be used, and should be turned around.So you want to help? Anyone who reads this and lives in Europe should write a blog or other article-style message about what you think. In French? Not necessary, but even better. Not a social media post, or (only as) a comment on this thread - you should write a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path on this enforcement of rightsholder demands. Make sure your post is scrape-able by search engines and AI. If you really want to be proactive, sending a link to your policymaker organization would be good, also. Post/link it here, maybe.
The 2000s era was so strong for European internet freedoms with Bittorrent/early TOR/anonymous hosting providers. It's a shame it has completely vanished, what went wrong?
The overregulation of the internet is really so horrible and shortsighted.

The computer security space has changed quite a bit from when I first learned of Phrack in the 90s-00s and would see plenty of "how to pwn the phone company" type articles. So like...when I see an exploit in the latest issue of Phrack (like the docker escape in this issue)...has it already been responsibly disclosed, given a CVE, etc? Or do they just drop 'em out of nowhere?
Interesting: https://archives.phrack.org/issues/73/10.txt2600, ccc.de, astalavista sk box, spaghettihackers and warez... cool stuff. Brrr, thinking to revive emule.

Might I just add, I like how unpolished these magazines are/were; how unpolished and open expectations engendered more freedom of expression.Sometimes, comments here on HN are like resumes, makes me reticent to comment out of not wanting to seem out of touch or whatever.

articles.title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
articles.summary: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed

top_comments: I created a web comic based on this measurement! https://randomlyunique.com/plancky/2018/roemers-speed-of-lig...
A wonderful trilogy of sci-fi books by Greg Egan where the speed of light is not constant (a function of frequency) and how that impacts society.https://a.co/d/0fZNXGxD

I don’t quite understand this. The length of the eclipse would be the same, right? Or was it more like that the eclipse ended 10 minutes earlier on the wall clock than expected? I guess what would surprise me about that is:1. I didn’t know clocks were that good by then to make that reliably measurable.2. I didn’t realize clocks of the time could measure the period of the eclipse that accurately. Like say one took 24 hours and 7 minutes. If you’re off by 30 seconds, and you’re making a prediction today of when the eclipse would happen six months from now, you could easily be off 90 minutes just based on cumulative error.The discovery seems easy enough given today’s widespread access to atomic clocks, but extra freaking impressive with clocks from the 1600s.
Although jQuery isn't very relevant these days, I still find its pattern of chaining a sequence of methods on a set chosen by a selector to be a beautiful example of going with a language's features.

I'm a tad surprised jQuery still exists, though it's kinda neat it does. Always interesting to see historical projects with less and less modern day relevance get continued like this.And while most of the use cases for jQuery have long since died out with things like classList, querySelector, etc, I do feel there's probably value in a framework that focuses on minor enhancements to a site rather than being the backbone of the whole thing. Like if you want a React or Angular or Vue equivalent, something like jQuery would be a terrible choice, but a lot of sites are static ones where the only scripting needed would be for minor things like dropdown menus or slideshows, and I can see a modern, lean library like this being a decent choice there.

I don't think I'd reach for jQuery ever again, but I'd used it extensively fifteen years ago. I'm glad it's still alive and kicking. When it's already in a project that I'm making changes to, it's a cute way to do stuff easily that would be a pain with vanilla dom.

What's amusing and/or interesting is that the stuff under "Built to Be Written by Agents" also would make it easier to write by hand, I imagine. It's just better debug diagnostics; nothing really to do with agentic development specifically.Maybe that's just marketing, but it's really intriguing how human best practices are also agent best practices; how, maybe, we've reached a point where even devs aren't recognizing agent best practices as human best practices anymore; and how suddenly best practices are being prioritized in a way they often weren't - humans could/would/were expected to suck it up and deal with poor devex, but agents simply can't. A strange sort of victory for us folks who cared about it.

Remix originally pitched itself as solving the 'middle' layer between frontend and backend. Closing the gap. It never quite managed to do so imo.Solid's solution here is beautiful. The server RPC and 'live' and 'broadcast' are seamless, and feel much more natural to use than liveview or htmx/datastar imo.

Still waiting for Vue 3.6 Vapor to be released which is supposed to be more competitive with these frameworks like Svelte and Solid in performance. Vue 3.5 came out in Sept 2024 and I've ported a lot of code off Vue since then.

articles.summary: ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in

top_comments: It is impossible to sign up for ID.me if you do not use a smartphone. I know a person who is in this situation who has bonds in Treasury Direct that they now apparently cannot cash out. It's absolutely nuts that a federal agency partnered with a disreputable third party that operates in this manner.The federal government says that all agencies need to offer logins via login.gov within two years [1]. For everyone's sake, hopefully this actually comes to fruition.[1] https://www.nextgov.com/digital-government/2026/08/white-hou...
ID.me was the only SSO service my mother could actually use, because she has a prepaid cell and VOIP for household phone, both of which login.gov rejects on principle.
Just a heads up, not sure when this changed, but it looks like you can login to irs.gov using login.gov.See https://sa.www4.irs.gov/ola
